title: Yaa Asantewaa, the Warrior Queen
author: Léxi
desc: En 1900, une reine mère ashanti mène la guerre contre l'Empire britannique pour protéger le Tabouret d'or.

p: In the Ashanti kingdom, in today's Ghana, there is a very special object: the Golden Stool.

It is a small wooden seat covered with gold. But it is not a normal chair. Nobody sits on it, not even the king. The Ashanti believe that the Golden Stool holds the soul of the whole nation — the people of the past, the present and the future.
According to legend, the Golden Stool came down from the sky about three hundred years ago and landed on the knees of the first great king, Osei Tutu.
For the Ashanti, protecting the Golden Stool means protecting their identity.
Yaa Asantewaa was born around 1840 in Ejisu, a town in the Ashanti kingdom. She was a farmer. She grew crops and had one daughter.
Later, her brother became chief of Ejisu, and she became the Queen Mother. In Ashanti culture, the Queen Mother is very important. She gives advice to the chief and helps choose new leaders.
At that time, the British wanted to control the Gold Coast. In 1896, they sent the Ashanti king, Prempeh I, into exile, far away on the Seychelles islands. Many Ashanti leaders went with him.
The kingdom was without its king. The people were angry and afraid.
In March 1900, the British governor, Frederick Hodgson, came to Kumasi. He made a terrible demand: "Bring me the Golden Stool. I want to sit on it."
For the Ashanti, this was the worst insult possible.
The chiefs met in secret. Some were afraid. The British had guns and a big army. Some chiefs said it was better to pay and accept.
Then Yaa Asantewaa stood up. She was about sixty years old. Her words are still famous today:
"If you, the men of Ashanti, will not go forward, then we will. We, the women, will. I shall call upon my fellow women. We will fight!"
The men were ashamed. They decided to fight, and they chose Yaa Asantewaa as the leader of the war.

chapters.t: The War of the Golden Stool
p: The war began in March 1900. Yaa Asantewaa's warriors surrounded the British fort in Kumasi for several months.
It was a long and difficult war. In the end, the British sent thousands of soldiers. Yaa Asantewaa was captured and sent into exile in the Seychelles. She died there in 1921, far from her home.
But the British never got the Golden Stool. The Ashanti hid it well, and it was never taken.
In 1924, King Prempeh I came back from exile. And the Golden Stool is still in Kumasi today.
Yaa Asantewaa is a hero in Ghana. There is a school with her name, a museum in Ejisu, and every year people remember her. She showed the world that courage has no age and no gender.
